items.title: US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system
items.originalTitle: US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system
items.summary: Trust Automation has completed a US Army operational assessment of its Small-Unmanned Air Defense System (SUADS) during a National Training Center rotation at Fort Irwin, California. Conducted with the 703rd Brigade Support Battalion, 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 3rd Infantry Division, the assessment evaluated SUADS in a large-scale combat operations training environment under ongoing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threats.

evidenceRecords.text: Trust Automation has completed a US Army operational assessment of its Small-Unmanned Air Defense System (SUADS) during a National Training Center rotation at Fort Irwin, California.

Conducted with the 703rd Brigade Support Battalion, 2nd Armored Brigade Combat Team, 3rd Infantry Division, the assessment evaluated SUADS in a large-scale combat operations training environment under ongoing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threats.

During the rotation, Trust Automation’s SUADS detected and engaged UAS between approximately two and six kilometres away, with potential coverage extending to approximately seven kilometres under favourable conditions, the company said in a 12 October press release.
Trust Automation’s integrated system combined radar, electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors, NINJA and DroneBuster technologies.
SUADS brings multiple sensors and effectors into a single integrated system while enabling individual technologies to be added or upgraded as capabilities and threats evolve.
Trust Automation is also developing a mobile SUADS variant to support tactical units where forces move frequently.
For more information Trust Automation The September issue of the 2026 Unmanned Airspace Global Counter-UAS Systems Directory is now available.
The post US Army assesses Trust Automation’s integrated drone defence system first appeared on Unmanned airspace .
Interview participants were not aware of any enemy UAS that penetrated the defended area as a threat within the identified operational ranges without first being detected by the system.

MAJ Patrick Smith, Battalion Executive Officer said the system consistently provided layered surveillance, early warning, positive target identification and electronic defeat of hostile UAS before enemy systems could successfully conduct reconnaissance, target acquisition or attack missions.

items.title: Army plans ‘rodeo’ to round up supply-chain problems
items.originalTitle: Army plans ‘rodeo’ to round up supply-chain problems
items.summary: The U.S. Army is planning a \"rodeo\" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service\u2019s acting chief said today.\u00a0 \u201cWe need to strain the nation's larger industrial base. We're going to stress-test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes, and see where it breaks,\u201d Adam Telle said at the Association of the U.S. Army\u2019s annual conference in Washington, D.C. Production bottlenecks and a lack of suppliers for many key parts have plagued the Army for decades.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Army is planning a "rodeo" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service’s acting chief said today.

The U.S. Army is planning a \"rodeo\" to round up problems that slow the deployment of new weapons, and rope in new ways to improve supply chains and make parts in more places, the service\u2019s acting chief said today.\u00a0
\u201cWe need to strain the nation's larger industrial base.

We're going to stress-test the supply chain, the manufacturing processes, and see where it breaks,\u201d Adam Telle said at the Association of the U.S. Army\u2019s annual conference in Washington, D.C.
Production bottlenecks and a lack of suppliers for many key parts have plagued the Army for decades.
The Government Accountability Office, among others, has detailed many breaking points.

But, Telle said, those reports don\u2019t capture how bad the problem could become as the Army seeks new drones and counterdrone weapons with components made by companies far from the service\u2019s control.
For instance, he said, the Army needs to \u201cmake millions\u201d of one-way attack drones.\u00a0
\u201cIt may look simple, but it's a flying supply chain.
If somebody else controls one part, they can break the whole thing,\u201d the acting chief said.
Parts for such drones are largely made in China, which uses its market dominance to help other autocratic states like Russia and Iran attack U.S. forces and partner militaries in Europe.\u00a0
Telle, who did not name any adversary, said that \u201can economy that's an extension of the national-security apparatus\u201d can be \u201cruthlessly efficient\u201d in deploying weapons.\u00a0

The acting Army chief listed steps the Pentagon has taken to overcome bureaucratic sluggishness in developing and deploying new technologies, such as pushing more acquisition authority down to battalion-level commanders, getting more self-sustained power on U.S. bases, and introducing a program to allow private companies to test new weapons on U.S. Army ranges.

items.title: Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026
items.originalTitle: Hanwha Highlights M38/M48 MUSV and Containerized Munitions at AUSA 2026
items.summary: At AUSA 2026, Hanwha Defense USA featured a model of the M38 MUSV made in partnership with Magnet Defense, with the parent design vessel recently arriving at National Harbor just outside of Washington D.C. following previous rounds of testing at sea. Hanwha’s Kevin Schoonover provided insight into the ongoing program, including several of Hanwha’s munitions offering destined to outfit the vessel and other platforms, alongside greater detail pertaining to the partnership with Magnet Defense.

evidenceRecords.text: At AUSA 2026, Hanwha Defense USA featured a model of the M38 MUSV made in partnership with Magnet Defense, with the parent design vessel recently arriving at National Harbor just outside of Washington D.C. following previous rounds of testing at sea.

Hanwha’s Kevin Schoonover provided insight into the ongoing program, including several of Hanwha’s munitions offering destined to outfit the vessel and other platforms, alongside greater detail pertaining to the partnership with Magnet Defense.
Schoonover also highlighted how the M38 is the primary testing vehicle for the class standing at 38 meters long, with future production upgrading to the larger 48 meter standard found on the M48.
To this end steel has been cut for the first M48, with production coinciding with continued testing of the original M38.
Naval News previously reported on the partnership between Hanwha and Magnet Defense , primarily geared towards breaching the emerging U.S. USV market.
Like similar sized USVs, the M38 also features the capability to carry containerized payloads related to multiple missions, including strike, reconnaissance, and electronic warfare.
Magent Defense claims the M38 has already demonstrated its range of 17,000 nautical miles on multiple tests, including a trip across the Pacific to American Samoa in up to conditions of Sea State 9 .
This has been part of a bid to introduce the M38 to overseas markets, including those beyond the U.S.’s MUSV program and Korean operation.
M38’s Weapons A scale model of the 40 foot containerized version of K-VLS II at Hanwha’s AUSA booth.
Joining the M38 at Hanwha’s booth, the company showcased offerings for both containerized Multiple Launch Rocket Systems (MLRS) and containerized Vertical Launch Systems (VLS).

When paired with M38, the vessel can carry up to 4 of the 20 foot long containerized munition packages, 2 of the 40 foot long options, or a combination of a pair of 20 foot containers and a singular 40 foot container A containerized version of the Chunmoo family of MLRS systems constitutes one of the 20 foot options, utilizing the same munitions and launch mechanisms found on the truck based version.

items.title: Ukraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time
items.originalTitle: Ukraine is building a patchwork antiballistic defense, one stopgap at a time
items.summary: Kyiv is assembling a patchwork of antiballistic air defense solutions, each piece on a different clock: Rounds transferred from allied stocks for this winter, imported systems and licensed production that will begin to matter over the next several years, and Freyja, a Ukrainian-European interceptor still in development. Stockpile swaps The fastest fix depends on allies sharing existing stockpiles, a request Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara put forward at his first Ukraine Defense Contact Group meeting with allies on Sept. 8.

items.title: European U740 Variant Of The XQ-58A Valkyrie Has Flown
items.originalTitle: European U740 Variant Of The XQ-58A Valkyrie Has Flown
items.summary: Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have completed the first flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, a Europeanized version of the XQ-58A Valkyrie , advancing their bid to deliver a combat-ready system to Germany by 2029. The flight comes as the German Air Force, or Luftwaffe, moves toward acquiring a new class of jet-powered combat drones, in what could become a major shift in the country’s traditionally limited armed-uncrewed-aircraft capabilities.

evidenceRecords.text: Airbus and Kratos Defense & Security Solutions have completed the first flight of the U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft, a Europeanized version of the XQ-58A Valkyrie , advancing their bid to deliver a combat-ready system to Germany by 2029.

The flight comes as the German Air Force, or Luftwaffe, moves toward acquiring a new class of jet-powered combat drones, in what could become a major shift in the country’s traditionally limited armed-uncrewed-aircraft capabilities.

The ride of the Valkyrie With the successful first flight of the Airbus U740 Valkyrie in Europe, we are one step closer to introducing an operational uncrewed Collaborative Combat Aircraft (CCA) to the German and other European Armed Forces.

The flight achieved all… pic.twitter.com/S2sFrtdmGA — Airbus Defence (@AirbusDefence) October 12, 2026 The flight took place at an unnamed test facility in northern Europe, Airbus announced on October 12.
The aircraft conducted a rocket-assisted takeoff, maneuvers at different altitudes, and flight at speeds of up to Mach 0.8.
The U740 Valkyrie uncrewed combat aircraft is prepared for launch.

Airbus The next phase will introduce Airbus’ Multi-platform Autonomous Reconfigurable and Secure (MARS) mission system, which is intended to provide the aircraft’s European-controlled software and mission-management architecture.
Airbus says MARS will support autonomous operations and coordination between multiple uncrewed aircraft while retaining human oversight of critical decisions.
The U740 is based on Kratos’ American-developed XQ-58A , an uncrewed aircraft designed as a relatively affordable combat platform.
The U740 Valkyrie on its launch trailer.
Airbus Published performance figures for the U740 include a maximum takeoff weight of around 3,000 kilograms (6,600 pounds).
A U.S. Marine Corps XQ-58A Valkyrie conducts a test flight with a U.S. Air Force F-16.

items.title: India sells air defense missiles to Tajikistan, Turkmenistan in Central Asia push
items.originalTitle: India sells air defense missiles to Tajikistan, Turkmenistan in Central Asia push
items.summary: NEW DELHI — India has sold its homegrown, short-range surface-to-air missile system called Akash, to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan gaining a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to expand its defense exports. Analysts say these countries are turning to India to reduce their reliance on Russia, one of the region’s main arms suppliers, whose defense resources are strained by its war with Ukraine.

evidenceRecords.text: NEW DELHI — India has sold its homegrown, short-range surface-to-air missile system called Akash, to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan gaining a foothold in Central Asia as it seeks to expand its defense exports.
Analysts say these countries are turning to India to reduce their reliance on Russia, one of the region’s main arms suppliers, whose defense resources are strained by its war with Ukraine.

“They are looking for a way to diversify at a time when Russia is no longer active in defense markets as it increasingly looks inwards towards its domestic needs, reducing its capacity to export air defense systems, especially in large numbers,” Aleksei Zakharov, a fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi told Defense News.

“As a result, Central Asian countries are looking for possible alternatives.” Indian Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh confirmed the sales of the Akash surface-to-air missile system to Tajikistan and Turkmenistan earlier this month in an interview with news agency Asian New International.
India moves closer to a homegrown, long-range air defense In 2022, Armenia became India’s first foreign customer for the air defense system.
The Akash system can simultaneously engage multiple targets at ranges up to 25km according to the Defense Ministry.
Calling the system one of India’s “success stories,” Singh said: “It shows the maturing of our indigenous missile design and production system.

Confidence in the missile system got a boost after it was “battle-tested” in a real conflict, according to Zakharov and could encourage Central Asian buyers to consider other Indian hardware, such as artillery and radar systems, as growing geopolitical uncertainty prompts countries to broaden their supplier base.
“Certainly this can be an important first step for India’s entry into the defense markets of Central Asia.

“The Indian systems such as Akash are also cost-effective.” In fact, Armenia has emerged as India’s largest buyer of military equipment, signing defense contracts worth nearly $2 billion since 2020, according to reports.
Analysts say India’s outreach in Central Asia also aims to balance China’s growing influence in the region where Beijing has emerged as a major supplier of military equipment in recent years.

items.title: Raytheon tests new Coyote interceptor upgrades
items.originalTitle: Raytheon tests new Coyote interceptor upgrades
items.summary: Raytheon has completed three tests of its new Coyote Block 2C+RM interceptor upgrades to support the US military requirement to counter evolving drone threats. The Coyote Block 2C+RM upgrade builds on the current Coyote variants, which Raytheon says have intercepted hundreds of drones. The upgrade intends to integrate a rocket motor for faster launch and flight, along with a new seeker and warhead designed to defeat all classes of current and emerging drone threats.

items.title: Phantom Defense acquires Karakurt and integrates net launchers into C-UAS range
items.originalTitle: Phantom Defense acquires Karakurt and integrates net launchers into C-UAS range
items.summary: Ukrainian defence technology company Phantom Defense has announced the completion of its acquisition of the developer of Karakurt net launchers. The transaction involves the full acquisition of the business and its team. The Karakurt net deployment system enables the physical interception of uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) without kinetic impact. The device deploys a net over the target, entangling its rotors and preventing further flight. Enemy drones can be brought down in a condition suitable for examination or potential reuse in combat operations by Ukraine’s defence forces.

The systems are adapted for different carrier platforms and tactical scenarios.
For DJI Mavic, Matrice and Autel platforms (M3, M4, A4 variants), the system deploys a net vertically from above.
For FPV drones and specialised platforms, the system uses forward net deployment with a target retention mechanism to intercept moving targets at high speed.
Phantom Defense says military units have deployed more than 50,000 Karakurt kits over the past six months.

To collect operational data and further improve the technology, the company has introduced a programme offering free replacement of consumables to units that submit video evidence of successful enemy UAS interceptions.
The programme has already recorded more than 5,000 video-confirmed interceptions.

Research and technology investigations taking place aboard the space station benefit people on Earth and lay the groundwork for other agency deep space missions.

evidenceRecords.text: The latest iteration of Lockheed Martin’s PAC-3 family of missile interceptors is designed to bring extreme agility to bear against a diverse array of missile threats, Defense News learned.
The defense giant unveiled the PAC-3 Edge this Friday and debuted it at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, D.C., today.

It’s capable of being launched from the containerized launchers that are being sought after domestically and internationally, as well as our HIMARS FLEX, which is the offense and defense configuration of our traditional HIMARS vehicle,” Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Lockheed Martin Missiles and Fire Control Integrated Air and Missile Defense, told Defense News.
Lockheed in January announced a seven-year framework agreement to increase annual PAC-3 interceptor production from approximately 600 to 2,000.

Designed to defend against hypersonic and advanced missile threats, the unveiling of the PAC-3 Edge comes as the U.S. military’s reliance on costly interceptors against cheap munitions, particularly those deployed by Iran during Operation Epic Fury, has come under increased scrutiny over the past eight months.
The new PAC-3 Edge missile builds on the foundations of the PAC-3 MSE, Lockheed’s baseline missile, and pushes its abilities farther.

“This has additional attitude control motors that give it additional agility.” While the PAC-3 MSE uses a two-pulse solid rocket motor to speedily approach moving targets, the new system has multi-pulse motor designed by Northrop Grumman.
The company intends to begin testing the PAC-3 Edge in 2027 and have it ready to deploy by 2031, although Lockheed aims to have it ready earlier, Reynolds added.

evidenceRecords.text: CASA said respondents broadly supported the objectives of the three proposals, covering a risk-based approach to determine when a NOTAM is required for an area approval, relocating existing record keeping and information requirements, and nationally consistent remote pilot licence examinations.
Feedback highlighted the need for clear and consistent NOTAM decision making and practical implementation arrangements.
Respondents considered that this could reduce briefing workload and information overload, helping airspace users identify operationally important information.
Submissions also emphasised the importance of maintaining aviation safety.
Examples included emergency services, military activity, aerial work, mustering and other general aviation operations.
Some submissions indicated a preference for NOTAM publication to remain the default, or to continue for all drone and rocket operations.
Respondents consistently emphasised the need for clear and nationally consistent criteria for determining when a NOTAM is required.

Suggested factors included operating height and duration, proximity to aerodromes and flight paths, airspace classification, the likelihood of low-level crewed aircraft, the dimensions of the approved area and other available risk controls.
Some respondents also sought greater clarity about how NOTAM decisions would be documented and communicated.
Suggestions included recording whether a NOTAM is required in the area approval and maintaining a record of the basis for the decision.
Feedback also noted that unclear criteria could lead operators to submit precautionary NOTAM requests, potentially limiting the intended benefits of the proposal.
Respondents sought clarity about who would request or arrange NOTAM publication, applicable lead times, and how changes, cancellations and system outages would be managed.

PRESS RELEASE — Bloq Quantum today announced the launch of Bloq Maya, its flagship AI Agent designed to simplify and accelerate quantum computing for enterprises.
It’s built to solve a very specific problem: making quantum computing actually usable for enterprise quantum teams.
The launch of Bloq Maya addresses a critical bottleneck in the industry: translating complex theoretical quantum concepts into production-ready business solutions.
Bloq Maya functions as an intelligent AI partner.
Through a simple conversational interface, you can ask Maya to generate custom quantum circuits, build QUBOs, review algorithms, or generate optimized quantum code.
“Translating complex quantum workflows into production-ready enterprise applications remains a massive bottleneck for enterprises,” said Sreekuttan L S, Co-Founder and CEO of Bloq Quantum.

“Bloq Maya removes the friction so teams can go from an idea to a tested quantum use case up to 10x faster.” The platform integrates this agentic AI seamlessly into Bloq ‘s unified workspace, offering several key features: Low-Code Algorithm Library: Access to over 15 pre-built, advanced research-grade algorithms, including QKAN, PQK, QEMCMC, and QSVM.
Visual Circuit Studio: An intuitive visual builder for designing parameterized quantum circuits (PQCs), feature maps, and complex gate compositions without deep quantum coding.
Experiments Module: A streamlined environment for testing use cases against quantum algorithms.

Maritime operations are one focus of the collaboration, with EchoShield increasingly integrated aboard uncrewed surface vessels for maritime awareness and C-UAS missions.

PRESS RELEASE — QuDef, a Netherlands-based leader in quantum technology security, and The Thought Projects (TTP), a Singapore-based innovation leader in future-proof data security and Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security evaluation, today announced a strategic collaboration.
The two companies have signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) under which TTP will bring QuDef’s flagship SQOUT ® platform to Singapore and the broader Asia-Pacific market.
The collaboration aims to strengthen the security assurance ecosystem for quantum communication technologies and support the adoption of trusted quantum-safe solutions across the region.

As governments, critical infrastructure operators, telecommunications providers, and enterprises deploy QKD alongside post-quantum cryptography (PQC), the security of the deployed systems, not only of the underlying protocols, has become a strategic priority.

Bringing European quantum security expertise to Asia-Pacific SQOUT ® is QuDef’s threat intelligence and knowledge platform which is used for systematic threat and risk assessment of QKD products and quantum communication networks.

items.originalTitle: Sweden Formalizes Interim Submarine Training and Södermanland Lease for Poland
items.summary: Sweden has finalized formal contracts for Polish submarine crew training and the lease of the interim A17-class boat HMS Södermanland to Poland, paving the way for the future delivery of Saab A26 submarines. The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Navy have signed formal implementation contracts in the frame of Poland’s Orka submarine program. Building on the agreement for the procurement of three Saab A26 (Blekinge-class) submarines , the new accords finalize the framework for crew training and the lease of the interim submarine HMS Södermanland to the Polish Navy.

evidenceRecords.text: Sweden has finalized formal contracts for Polish submarine crew training and the lease of the interim A17-class boat HMS Södermanland to Poland, paving the way for the future delivery of Saab A26 submarines.
The Swedish Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and the Swedish Navy have signed formal implementation contracts in the frame of Poland’s Orka submarine program.

Building on the agreement for the procurement of three Saab A26 (Blekinge-class) submarines , the new accords finalize the framework for crew training and the lease of the interim submarine HMS Södermanland to the Polish Navy.
Training for the initial Polish submarine crews is already well underway in Karlskrona by the Royal Swedish Navy’s 1st Submarine Flotilla and the Naval Warfare Centre with FMV support.
“The training lasts for 18 months, which is the same training length as for a Swedish submarine crew” the Swedish Navy said its LinkedIn account .
The centerpiece of the interim agreement is the transfer and operation of HMS Södermanland .

Originally built as a Västergötland-class boat in the late 1980s, the vessel underwent a comprehensive mid-life upgrade that lengthened her hull and integrated an air-independent Stirling propulsion (AIP) system.
By leasing the boat, the Polish Navy gains vital hands-on experience operating a modern, Swedish-built AIP submarine ahead of the first A26 deliveries scheduled for 2031.
During the lease, the Swedish Navy will continue to provide foundational maintenance and sustainment support.

Alongside the interim boat arrangements, the wider Orka framework encompasses comprehensive weapon packages—featuring advanced heavy and light torpedoes—and lays the groundwork for shared underwater domain cooperation, such as potential synergies with Poland’s Ratownik submarine rescue vessel program.
With training advancing smoothly, Warsaw and Stockholm are firmly cementing a strategic underwater partnership designed to secure the Baltic for decades to come.

evidenceRecords.text: Lockheed Martin has unveiled the PAC-3 Edge, a new interceptor that would represent the top tier of the U.S. Army’s Patriot air defense missile family.

The missile is being developed to deliver greater performance against advanced threats than the current PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE), as the Army advances a competition for its next-generation interceptor.
The PAC-3 Edge displayed at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention.
Howard Altman The company says PAC-3 Edge will offer improved performance against increasingly challenging aerial threats, including advanced ballistic and hypersonic missiles.
The design builds on the PAC-3 MSE’s existing technology while incorporating a new seeker, an upgraded control system, and a more advanced solid rocket motor developed with Northrop Grumman.
In terms of appearance, PAC-3 Edge differs significantly from the PAC-3 MSE.
An overview of the improvements found on the PAC-3 MSE variant over its predecessors.
The Army previously abandoned its Lower-Tier Future Interceptor (LTFI) program in 2024, citing cost concerns, and instead emphasized incremental improvements to the existing PAC-3 MSE.
A PAC-3 interceptor seen at the moment of launch.

U.S. Department of Defense A More Capable Patriot Interceptor PAC-3 Edge is intended to preserve the advantages of the existing PAC-3 family while improving the missile’s ability to engage targets at longer ranges and higher altitudes.

Tim Cahill, president of Missiles and Fire Control (MFC) for Lockheed Martin, told TWZ that the same seeker technology that will be used in PAC-3 Edge will also find its way into future offensive and defensive systems going into the future.

To ensure greater agility, Jason Reynolds, vice president and general manager of Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) at Lockheed Martin, explained that the new missile adds a greater number of more capable attitude control motors (ACMs), compared to the PAC-3 MSE.

IonQ has agreed to buy cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion, expanding its security business as advances in quantum computing and artificial intelligence raise concerns about cyberattacks.
The transaction includes up to $150 million in additional payments tied to Elisity’s future performance, executives told The Wall Street Journal .
IonQ Chairman and CEO Niccolo de Masi told the newspaper that the acquisition reflects his expectation that companies will need stronger defenses as both technologies become more powerful.
“With Elisity and its team as part of IonQ , we will be well positioned to help customers protect critical infrastructure and enterprise networks throughout the transition to the quantum era.
IonQ is offering its customers a vertically integrated full-stack quantum platform across quantum computing, networking, sensing and cybersecurity.

Just as adding SkyWater Technology expanded IonQ’s capabilities in chip design, fabrication and packaging, Elisity will bring proven enterprise policy enforcement scale and deployment experience to our quantum security strategy and will give IonQ a strong growth platform to serve customers and create value for our shareholders,” Niccolo de Masi, Chairman and CEO of IonQ, said in a statement .
The Elisity agreement follows IonQ ’s $1.8 billion deal earlier this year to acquire chipmaker SkyWater Technology, likely its largest acquisition to date.

Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely. evidenceRecords.text: But beneath all these commercial incentives, there is real substance to disagreements about open models.

Those who are concerned about AI safety warn that open models can easily be misused by bad actors, whereas those who focus more on AI’s practical potential urge that this power should not sit behind the closed doors of just a few big companies, and that open models could help spread it more widely.
There are a range of ways to handle open models between banning them entirely and releasing them willy-nilly.
Deciding whether to support or limit the production of open models requires understanding those risks and benefits in depth.
What are the benefits of open models?
But any approach that a government or a society might take still involves trade-offs between safety and democratization.
A closed model, like the models that power ChatGPT and Claude, can only be accessed through a website, app, or API.
For this reason, people who take seriously the purported catastrophic risks posed by rogue agents, such as Dario Amodei, tend to be more skeptical of open models.

A few years ago, the debate about open models had an all-or-nothing framing: Either you supported open models because of their potential to fight concentration of power, or you rejected them because of the safety risks.
These days, however, people are expending a lot of effort to find some middle ground.
One way they are doing that is by devising techniques to mitigate the safety risks of open models.
If the risks of open models are less black-and-white than they might at first seem, so are the benefits.
Real openness—not only open weights, but also open training data and accessible hardware—could also bring more risks, of course.
But there are strategies for mitigating these risks.

evidenceRecords.text: SpaceX Cargo Dragon C211, making its fourth flight, launched successfully on Tuesday, Oct. 13, at 6:33 AM EDT (10:33 UTC) from Space Launch Complex 40 (SLC-40) at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida on the CRS-35 mission.
CRS-35 took a northeast trajectory after liftoff, placing the Cargo Dragon in an orbit inclined 51.6 degrees to the equator, the same inclination used by the Station.
See Also CRS-35 Updates ISS Section Click here to Join L2 Now that CRS-35 reachedorbit, Dragon will take just over 52 hours to rendezvous and dock with the Station’s Harmony module.

CRS-35 will carry 2,867 kg of cargo to the Station, including 593 kg of science experiments, 383 kg of crew supplies, 362 kg of vehicle hardware, 189 kg of spacewalk equipment, and 36 kg of computer resources.
This will improve the power supply margin to keep the ISS going through its final years and decommissioning, as the original solar arrays that launched with the Station are aging and degraded.
The Stellar Spheroids experiment carried aboard CRS-35. (Credit: NASA) Another experiment, ELF-Unconventional Glass 2, will form glass in microgravity using non-traditional elements.
CRS-35 is also carrying a collapsible contingency urinal test unit for the Artemis III mission aboard the Orion spacecraft, as well as a toilet dose pump and a pretreatment quality sensor.
CRS-35 will return one spacesuit to Earth for refurbishment, and the spacecraft will also return a urine processor pump assembly and a water processor filtration unit.
CRS-35 is the 113th Falcon 9 mission of 2026, and the 119th mission overall for SpaceX this year.

items.summary: Defense tech company Forterra introduced a new platform on Monday at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington that will allow service members to control different autonomous systems using one user interface. OASIS-OneLink builds upon Forterra’s OASIS-Fabric, a shared data network that allows unmanned machines to connect in communication-degraded environments where they can’t log onto a shared data grid.

evidenceRecords.text: Defense tech company Forterra introduced a new platform on Monday at the Association of the United States Army conference in Washington that will allow service members to control different autonomous systems using one user interface.
OASIS-OneLink builds upon Forterra’s OASIS-Fabric, a shared data network that allows unmanned machines to connect in communication-degraded environments where they can’t log onto a shared data grid.

“Requiring operators to start an integration process from scratch every time a new system is introduced is both inefficient and burdensome for the end user,” Phil Cotter, Forterra’s head of growth, told Military Times.
While Fabric provided a new way for machines to connect, OneLink provides a new way to control them.
New systems and pieces of technology come with their own operating systems and visual layouts, not unlike different computers or phones.

If a service member wants to control several different autonomous systems, or if a new one is introduced to the mix, they may have to learn a completely new user interface or remember several different ones while toggling between them.
But OASIS-OneLink would allow several different autonomous machines, potentially all from different companies, to be controlled using the same operating control framework, said Tuck.

The shared interface could also speed up the testing and evaluation phase before fielding new technology, since it would allow the Defense Department to focus on the performance of new autonomous systems and reduce time otherwise devoted to the tedious mastery of new controls.
The Army’s Joint Readiness Training Center has already begun using OASIS-OneLink to pilot unmanned systems, Forterra said.
Oasis-OneLink wasn’t the only shiny new toy the company showed off at AUSA.

The company unveiled a new autonomous ground vehicle that it created with Hypercraft, integrating its AutoDrive autonomous software platform to form a machine capable of carrying out high-risk missions without endangering soldiers’ lives.

items.originalTitle: Swinburne and IQM Partner on Quantum Research and Workforce Development
items.summary: Insider Brief Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers have formed a partnership to advance quantum research, technology development, education, and workforce training across Australia, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific. The collaboration will include joint training programs, internships, research projects, technology development, workshops, and exchanges for students, researchers, and staff.

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Brief Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers have formed a partnership to advance quantum research, technology development, education, and workforce training across Australia, Europe, and the Indo-Pacific.
The collaboration will include joint training programs, internships, research projects, technology development, workshops, and exchanges for students, researchers, and staff.

The partnership builds on complementary expertise in quantum theory, experimentation, and superconducting quantum computers, with Swinburne representatives visiting IQM ’s production facility in Espoo, Finland.

PRESS RELEASE — Swinburne University of Technology and IQM Quantum Computers , the global leader in superconducting quantum computers, are partnering to advance quantum science, technology, innovation and workforce development capability.
This new partnership will include collaborating in education, training, research engagement and technology development across Australia, Europe and the Indo-Pacific.

“Quantum technologies have the potential to transform industries and address some of the world’s most complex challenges,” says Swinburne ’s Deputy Vice-Chancellor, Research, Professor Karen Hapgood .

“This partnership with IQM reflects our shared commitment to strengthen quantum expertise, expand learning opportunities and support the growth of a skilled workforce.” The development of quantum technologies is a key priority for both Australia and Finland, and this partnership helps to foster the international pathway for collaboration.

Swinburne ‘s quantum expertise in theory and experimentation along with IQM ‘s reputation in producing working quantum computers, will not only enable technology uplift, but will also advance quantum talent in both countries.
“Australia and Finland are both building real quantum capability, not just talking about it,” said IQM ‘s Chief Global Affairs Officer and co-founder, Juha Vartiainen.

In addition, the partnership will also support collaborative research, technology translation and innovation, as well as staff, researcher and student exchanges between Swinburne and IQM , helping to advance the next generation of quantum talent.
The partnership was finalised after a delegation from Swinburne , representing Australia, attended the Finnish Quantum Days event in Jyväskylä, Finland.

“At the moment we have not made choices, the natural armament is Turkish but we also have activities with MBDA and small Italian industrial groups,” he said.

items.title: The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
items.originalTitle: The escalation in Yemen is a turning point
items.summary: Yemen is witnessing a major military escalation that has once again brought the western coast and the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to the forefront of regional developments. Operation Yemen’s Dawn, launched by the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government, has produced some results. Government forces have advanced towards the strait of Bab al-Mandeb and are now fighting against reinforced Houthi positions. Clashes continue in parts of Dhubab District and around Dhubab Airport.

evidenceRecords.text: Yemen is witnessing a major military escalation that has once again brought the western coast and the area around the Bab al-Mandeb strait to the forefront of regional developments.
Operation Yemen’s Dawn, launched by the forces loyal to the internationally recognised Yemeni government, has produced some results.
Government forces have advanced towards the strait of Bab al-Mandeb and are now fighting against reinforced Houthi positions.
Clashes continue in parts of Dhubab District and around Dhubab Airport.
Fighting has concentrated around Bab al-Mandeb because of its strategic position in global trade and energy flows.

It is especially significant to the parties to the Yemeni conflict because control of the coastline, islands and surrounding highlands offers varying capabilities for surveillance, military deployment and threats to maritime traffic.
An advance along the coast may enable government forces to retake key positions and restrict the Houthis’ space for manoeuvre.
However, it does not, by itself, guarantee the security of the strait or eliminate threats to navigation.
Even if the Houthis lose coastal positions, they could still retain their ability to launch attacks in the Red Sea.

Threats to maritime traffic do not necessarily depend on direct control of the strait; they also depend on the availability of missiles, drones, launch platforms, supply networks and the ability to operate from other locations.

In this context, three distinct levels must be differentiated: retaking coastal positions, consolidating military control over them and establishing a sustainable capacity to secure the strait and its surrounding area.
Confusing these levels may lead either to an exaggerated assessment of the operation’s results or to an underestimation of the adversary’s ability to continue fighting.

items.title: Alice & Bob Decodes LDPC-Cat Codes on GPUs With NVIDIA NVQLink
items.originalTitle: Alice & Bob Decodes LDPC-Cat Codes on GPUs With NVIDIA NVQLink
items.summary: Insider Link Alice & Bob demonstrated GPU decoding of its LDPC-cat error-correction codes using NVIDIA NVQLink and synthetic data, a step toward scalable error correction for cat-qubit quantum computers. The proof of concept used Quantum Machines’ control hardware and showed improved decoding efficiency when processing multiple sets of error measurements in parallel. PRESS RELEASE — Alice & Bob , a leader in fault-tolerant quantum computing, today shared results from implementing GPUs to decode its LDPC-cat architecture using NVIDIA NVQLink .

evidenceRecords.text: Insider Link Alice & Bob demonstrated GPU decoding of its LDPC-cat error-correction codes using NVIDIA NVQLink and synthetic data, a step toward scalable error correction for cat-qubit quantum computers.
The proof of concept used Quantum Machines’ control hardware and showed improved decoding efficiency when processing multiple sets of error measurements in parallel.
PRESS RELEASE — Alice & Bob , a leader in fault-tolerant quantum computing, today shared results from implementing GPUs to decode its LDPC-cat architecture using NVIDIA NVQLink .

The proof of concept using synthetic data is the first time LDPC-cat codes have been decoded on GPUs via the low-latency, high throughput NVQLink architecture, and moves the company a step closer to fast, scalable error correction for its cat-qubit quantum computers.

Alice & Bob assessed the feasibility of GPU decoding for LDPC-cat codes using an NVQLink connection with Quantum Machines’ OPX1000 and Open Acceleration Stack, a modular framework that couples the controller directly to GPUs and other classical processors with microsecond-scale roundtrip latency.
LDPC-cat codes were developed by Alice & Bob for its cat-qubit architecture and first introduced in the paper “ LDPC-cat codes for low-overhead quantum computing in 2D” published in January 2025.
Alice & Bob will now optimize the pipeline, the chain of steps that carry the measurement data through NVQLink to the GPU, to enable the performance needed for real-time decoding.
Showing that our LDPC-cat codes can be decoded on NVIDIA GPUs with existing tools is encouraging for scaling, because it means decoding capacity can grow with the machine.
The next step is making it fast enough to keep pace with the quantum computer, and we’re working with NVIDIA to get there,” said Juliette Peyronnet, US GM Alice & Bob .

“ Alice & Bob ’s work shows how NVQLink can in fact accelerate the real-time decoding needed to turn cat qubits into fault tolerant quantum-GPU supercomputers.” This collaboration builds on the existing relationship between the two companies.
In June 2025, the companies announced integration of NVIDIA CUDA-Q into Dynamiqs, Alice & Bob’s QPU simulation library, enabling GPU-accelerated quantum simulations.

WISeSat.Space has access to nine active low-Earth-orbit satellites and targets a 100-satellite sovereign constellation by 2033, subject to financing, technical development, regulatory approvals, and launch availability.

PRESS RELEASE — WISeSat.Space (Nasdaq: SAIQ) (“WISeSat.Space” or the “Company”) today outlined its strategy to integrate post-quantum cryptography (“PQC”) into its next-generation satellite communications and Internet of Things (“IoT”) architecture, supporting the migration objectives established by U.S. Executive Order 14412, Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks.

The Company is developing a security architecture designed to protect communications, digital identities and satellite operations against both conventional cyberattacks and emerging quantum-computing threats.

“Security is a core differentiator in our strategy to build a satellite communications business serving governments, enterprises and critical infrastructure operators,” said Carlos Moreira, Founder and CEO of WISeSat.Space.

By integrating post-quantum technologies across connected devices, ground infrastructure and satellites, we aim to strengthen our competitive position, address demand for secure, sovereign communications and create long-term shareholder value.” Following its October 2026 business combination and Nasdaq listing, WISeSat.Space closed a $10 million PIPE investment led by SEALSQ to accelerate the development of its quantum-resilient space architecture.
Practical Applications Across Space and Earth WISeSat.Space is developing its architecture around several applications where communications security and long-term data protection are essential.

The Gulf nation announced it was suspending flights from Riyadh, its second busiest airport, after Houthi missiles killed 13 people on Saturday and left more than 300 injured.
Saudi state TV broadcast CCTV footage that showed passengers deluged in smoke and falling masonry as they queued at the airport terminal to board a plane just as the Houthi missile struck.
More missiles were fired at Saudi Arabian cities by the Houthis on Monday, Saudi Arabian’s military spokesperson said.
The country has pressed ahead with the 25th WPC Energy Conference in Riyadh, hoping to project an image of normality.
But some senior oil executives did not attend or appeared virtually.

The Saudi energy minister, Abdulaziz bin Salman, told the conference that “fear has no place in the Saudi lexicon”, emphasising the resilience of the kingdom’s energy system and the determination of its people to confront crises.

Amin Nasser, the president and chief executive of Aramco, said Saudi Arabia had invested deeply in protecting its supplies, but “no nation, even one as capable and confident as ours, can safeguard them alone.”
An urgent review is under way as to how Houthi missiles are repeatedly penetrating badly stretched Saudi air defences.
Schoolchildren and some office workers were advised to work from home.
The Houthis have also targeted the city of Khamis Mushait, and the King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

From above, the mere appearance of a curious geologic feature in Western Australia is enough to cause a fright.
The aptly named Spider Crater, the product of a meteorite impact followed by hundreds of millions of years of erosion, sprawls across the landscape in the country’s Kimberley region .
The OLI (Operational Land Imager) on the NASA-USGS Landsat 9 satellite captured this image of the crater on September 20, 2026.
The full impact structure has an oval shape measuring about 13 kilometers by 11 kilometers (8 miles by 7 miles), with the spiderlike central portion measuring about 4 kilometers (2.5 miles) across.
Geologists believe the unusual arachnoid pattern is the remnant of a central uplift , the raised portion of the crater floor that formed in the rebound of the initial impact shock.
The light-colored “legs” are sandstone ridges that have endured while other rock layers in the impact zone have eroded away.

evidenceRecords.text: General Dynamics Land Systems (GDLS) has offered the first official look at its proposal to replace the U.S. Army’s Bradley Fighting Vehicles, called the Wolf.
The Wolf is one of two designs competing to become the Army’s future XM30 Mechanized Infantry Combat Vehicle (MICV).

GDLS is showing the one-eighth-scale model of Wolf, seen at the top of this story and made by a company called KiwiMill , at the Association of the U.S. Army’s (AUSA) main annual convention, at which TWZ is in attendance .
It has already been established that Wolf is a further evolution of the GDLS’ Griffin III design, which was first shown publicly at AUSA back in 2018.
Griffin III was derived from the ASCOD 2 infantry fighting vehicle, for which Spain was the launch customer, and which is now entering service in Latvia.
The U.S. Army’s now-cancelled M10 Booker ‘light tank’ and the British Army’s much-troubled Ajax are also members of this broader family of armored vehicles.
GDLS/KiwiMill The design of the Wolf, at least based on the model, is substantially different from the earlier Griffin III demonstrator.

items.originalTitle: Mangroves and mud: Inside the Army jungle school’s notorious ‘Green Mile’
items.summary: The soldiers, some wearing days-old green face paint, had congregated amongst the moist fauna to complete their final task in the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama: The Green Mile. The notorious event — in the thick of Panama’s “Green Hell” — is the 18-day course’s culminating exercise, testing participants’ newly learned jungle maneuver techniques, survival measures and fighting skills. By that point in the course, the soldiers had run a days-long jungle reconnaissance and attack operation.

evidenceRecords.text: The soldiers, some wearing days-old green face paint, had congregated amongst the moist fauna to complete their final task in the U.S. Army’s Jungle Operations Training Course in Panama: The Green Mile.

The notorious event — in the thick of Panama’s “Green Hell” — is the 18-day course’s culminating exercise, testing participants’ newly learned jungle maneuver techniques, survival measures and fighting skills.
By that point in the course, the soldiers had run a days-long jungle reconnaissance and attack operation.
The course in 2025 returned to Panama at Base Aeronaval Cristóbal Colón, formerly known as the U.S. Army’s Fort Sherman, decades after it was originally shuttered.
The new course is a joint U.S.-Panamanian partnership, with Panamanian instructors leading lessons on jungle survival.
Squads in the September course had participants from across the U.S. force, including those from the Army, Marine Corps and Space Force.
Some squads had Panamanian soldiers.
That portion of the field exercise was complete, and perhaps to the howler monkey’s dismay, so were the soldiers’ attempts to stay quiet.
With staggered start times, each squad took off running down a soggy, uneven path.
Other countries, such as Colombia, have expressed interest in sending soldiers in the near future.
In classes with Panamanian students, instruction is given in English and Spanish.
When the course is English-only, the duration shrinks to 12 days, but without partners, officials say U.S. students can miss out on opportunities to connect with other forces.

items.summary: University of Pennsylvania researchers have used a photonic chip to transfer a winding pattern in quantum light that survived noise even after entanglement disappeared, which they say could help develop quantum networks. The team suggests this experiment could be an initial step on the path toward more resilient links between those extremely sensitive quantum systems.

evidenceRecords.text: University of Pennsylvania researchers have used a photonic chip to transfer a winding pattern in quantum light that survived noise even after entanglement disappeared, which they say could help develop quantum networks.
The team suggests this experiment could be an initial step on the path toward more resilient links between those extremely sensitive quantum systems.

The study, published in Nature Physics , demonstrates a way to create and manipulate quantum skyrmions, which are structured patterns in light whose overall winding can remain stable even as their underlying quantum state deteriorates.
In this case, these light patterns can retain their overall winding even as noise degrades their quantum state.
According to the study, the silicon nitride chip combined components that generated photon pairs, routed the photons and shaped the light into skyrmions.

Connecting quantum computers and other quantum devices is challenging because noise — which can include anything from heat to cosmic rays — can weaken the delicate relationships that carry quantum information, making it difficult to move that information reliably between systems.
The scientists preserved a particular measurable property of the light, rather than showing that an entire quantum state could be transmitted intact after entanglement was lost.
They point out that the experiment does not establish a practical advantage for quantum state transfer.

A Pattern That Holds Its Shape A photon, which is a particle of light, has a quantum state that can include polarization — the orientation and motion of light’s electric field — and spatial properties associated with how the light’s wavefront is arranged.
In these skyrmions, the orientation of light’s electric field changes from place to place, forming a winding pattern.

items.summary: Anthropic is battling large-scale distillation attacks on its Claude models. In these attacks, companies systematically copy an AI model's capabilities to train their own, smaller models. Anthropic says its new defenses have cut the volume of extracted reasoning tokens, the model's internal chain-of-thought steps, by 90 to 99 percent. Attackers use networks of hundreds of thousands of fake accounts to pull it off. Anthropic names Chinese companies Zhipu and Moonshot as participants.

evidenceRecords.text: Anthropic says it has cut the extraction of Claude's internal reasoning tokens by 90 to 99 percent.
The article Anthropic says it cut Claude reasoning token theft by up to 99% in fight against industrial-scale distillation appeared first on The Decoder .
Anthropic is battling large-scale distillation attacks on its Claude models.
In these attacks, companies systematically copy an AI model's capabilities to train their own, smaller models.
Anthropic says its new defenses have cut the volume of extracted reasoning tokens, the model's internal chain-of-thought steps, by 90 to 99 percent.
Attackers use networks of hundreds of thousands of fake accounts to pull it off.
Anthropic names Chinese companies Zhipu and Moonshot as participants.
Zhipu allegedly siphoned cyber capabilities from leading US models for its GLM-5.3 model, while Moonshot secretly routed queries through Claude.
The stolen capabilities could end up in foreign military and surveillance systems.
Anthropic now restricts access to Claude's internal reasoning steps, runs a classifier that detects extraction attempts, and automatically bans flagged accounts.
Tens of thousands have already been banned.
Anthropic is calling on other AI developers to adopt similar protections, although the company admits that legitimate users are getting caught up in the process too.
Source: Anthropic / Distillation Defenses

The article Anthropic study warns that small AI models could soon replicate across everyday devices appeared first on The Decoder .

Anthropic researchers tested whether small language models could spread on their own across poorly secured consumer devices like smart TVs or connected home appliances and set themselves up on unfamiliar hardware.
In tests using off-the-shelf $55 TV boxes, the GLM-5.2 model already completed the full replication chain across all eight test nodes.

Small AI models may be just months away from copying themselves across poorly secured consumer devices, according to a new Anthropic study.
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warns of potential damages in the hundreds of billions of dollars.
An AI model that copies itself from device to device, sets itself up, and keeps spreading.
Until now, this kind of risk was mainly tied to data centers.
But a new study by Anthropic researchers William Zhou and Daniel Freeman suggests it could work just as well across cheap consumer hardware.
The researchers wanted to find out whether small AI models can already spread on their own across poorly secured IoT devices like smart TVs, smart refrigerators, or robot vacuums.
An "AI worm" like this would carry its model weights as part of the malware payload and run inference directly on the compromised hardware.
Unlike traditional malware, it could explore unfamiliar hardware on its own and configure itself to run there.
To test whether this is feasible, the researchers ran the Gemma4-26B-A4B model distributed across 15 off-the-shelf Android TV boxes.

PRESS RELEASE — Quantum Design Oxford today announces that Dr Chunyu Guo , W2 Research Group Leader at the Max Planck Institute for the Structure and Dynamics of Matter , Hamburg, Germany has been awarded the 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize .

The Award recognises Dr Guo’s contributions to understanding the quantum behaviour of kagome metals and his discovery of many-body quantum interference and long-range coherent charge transport in strain-minimised microstructures under high magnetic fields.
“I am truly honored to receive the Nicholas Kurti Science Prize and to join its distinguished group of past recipients.

Matthew Martin, Managing Director at Quantum Design Oxford , said, “It is always an absolute pleasure to award the Nicholas Kurti prize, and we at Quantum Design Oxford are proud to support young scientists such as Dr Guo.

His work exemplifies the spirit of this prize, and underpins the importance of curiosity-driven and conceptually bold research in advancing the field of quantum materials science and condensed matter physics.” The Nicholas Kurti Science Prize for Europe promotes and recognises the novel work of young scientists working in the fields of low temperatures and/or high magnetic fields or surface science.
The 2026 Nicholas Kurti Science Prize selection committee is co-chaired by Professor Richard Haley (Lancaster University) and Dr Natalia Ares (University of Oxford).

The Middle East and Central Asia is the only region that is expected to experience negative growth in 2026.

evidenceRecords.text: The European Commission says Cyprus is ready to join the Schengen Area.
Cyprus is closer than ever to joining the Schengen Area.
After years of preparations and the implementation of 120 technical recommendations, Nicosia received a positive assessment from the European Commission in July, confirming its technical readiness.
The recommendations, issued as part of EU evaluations dating back to 2021, covered areas including border controls, visa policy, access to European security databases and police cooperation.
Their implementation required technological upgrades as well as legislative and administrative reforms.

On October 1, Cyprus's Deputy Minister for Migration and International Protection, Nicholas Ioannides, confirmed that "all recommendations made by the European Commission are now considered to have been implemented."
According to Ioannides, Cyprus is technically ready to join Schengen, with the next step being to secure the necessary political agreement.
However, a positive technical assessment alone is not enough for Cyprus to join the Schengen Area.
This unique arrangement poses a challenge to Schengen membership, as the Republic of Cyprus does not exercise effective control along the entire length of the line.
At the same time, Nicosia rejects any arrangement that could turn the Green Line into an external border, either legally or even symbolically.
"The issue raised by some Schengen countries is that the Republic of Cyprus does not control the entire Green Line.

It may control the crossing points, but there are also open stretches of land," Dr. Nasia Hadjigeorgiou, associate professor of Transitional Justice and Human Rights at the School of Law of UCLan Cyprus, told DW.

Another obstacle to Cyprus's Schengen ambitions is the presence of the British Sovereign Base Areas of Akrotiri and Dhekelia, which remained under UK sovereignty when Cyprus gained independence in 1960.
Cyprus's accession to Schengen was among the issues discussed.

items.originalTitle: Simulating student learning for better AI tutoring
items.summary: Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning. Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners. The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage. evidenceRecords.text: At a glance StudentSim is a research system for evaluating and improving AI tutors before they are tested with real learners; it is not a product, is not deployed in classrooms, and is not intended to replace teachers AI tutoring tools need feedback from students to improve, but collecting that feedback through human studies is slow, costly, and difficult to scale StudentSim trains personalized AI student simulators from publicly available, de-identified learner records, with one simulator adapted to each student The work evaluates simulators along two education-grounded dimensions: whether
A tutor needs to know what happens after the guidance reaches a student.
Knowledge tracing and behavior prediction models are grounded in real learning records and can estimate a student’s current knowledge, skills, and learning habits.
Importantly, the goal is not to replace teachers or classroom learning.
Instead, StudentSim helps researchers evaluate and improve AI tutoring systems during the research and development process before testing them with real learners.
The research uses only publicly available learner datasets released for research use with de-identified records; no personally identifying information is used at any stage.
Traditional student modeling approaches face a different limitation.
Many of these models, however, were not designed to take natural-language tutor guidance as input.
They can help describe what a student has done, but they do not always tell us how a student would respond to a particular explanation, hint, or Socratic question.
In a chess tutor reinforcement learning study, the tutor receives a position and a real student’s previous wrong move, then generates guidance.
The student simulator’s own parameters are held fixed during this process, and it reads the guidance and produces a revised move.

The study compares three conditions: a supervised fine-tuned tutor with no reinforcement learning, a tutor trained with GPT-5.4 as the simulated student reward source, and a tutor trained with StudentSim as the reward source.
All conditions use the same tutor policy, supervised starting point, and reinforcement learning setup.
Human chess experts then evaluate the tutor responses blind to condition.
The StudentSim reward produces the highest-rated tutor on all reported dimensions.
The tutor trained with StudentSim reaches 90.5% accuracy, compared with 75.7% for the no-RL baseline and 71.6% for the GPT-5.4 reward condition.
It also receives higher ratings for guidance quality and personalization.
The result is a proof of concept that student simulators trained on real learner data can provide useful feedback for improving AI tutors.
StudentSim does not remove the need for real learners in education research.

evidenceRecords.text: The U.S. Air Force will buy data collected by WindBorne Systems‘ fleet of autonomous weather balloons under a new contract that could be worth nearly $50 million to the startup.

WindBorne currently has about 700 weather balloons flying around the globe, collecting atmospheric sensor readings that the company sells to customers and also feeds into its own AI weather forecasting model.
WindBorne, founded in 2015 and based in Redwood City, California, is one of the first organizations to directly feed empirical data into a deep-learning weather model.

The company has worked closely with the U.S. government, particularly the National Weather Service and the U.S. Air Force and Navy, but this is the single-largest contract the company has participated in.
The contract is worth up to $49 million, but the Air Force pays only as it needs data.
It can place orders for specific regions at specific times.
So far, it has ordered $1.7 million worth, and executives expect more orders to follow.

“This is largely a vehicle through which continued growth of the constellation can be supported, as well as some work on research and development to continue to improve the hardware and performance of the balloons,” WindBorne co-founder and CTO Andrey Sushko told TechCrunch.

He added that the contract, which was awarded without competitive bidding, is “a determination by the government that for this capability of collecting global data, we were the only company able to provide it in the way that met their needs for these operations.”
WindBorne CEO John Dean told TechCrunch in August that the company had raised a $37 million Series B round to continue scaling its business.

Earlier this summer, the company released the latest version of its forecasting model, WeatherMesh 6, which it says provides more accurate forecasts than the traditional model run by the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which simulates the atmosphere using the laws of physics.
In August WindBorne became the first organization to send an unpowered flight system — one with no engine — to collect data in the eye of a typhoon.
The company maneuvers its balloons by adjusting their altitude, bleeding air, or dropping sand carried as ballast, to send the vehicles into winds that take them where they need to go.

evidenceRecords.text: Elsight wants to change that with a new positioning technology designed to help uncrewed systems determine their location even when GPS is unavailable, jammed, or spoofed. more…
GPS has become such a routine part of flying a drone that it’s easy to forget how vulnerable it can be.
Jam a satellite signal, feed a receiver fake coordinates, and an autonomous aircraft or ground vehicle could suddenly struggle to figure out where it is.
Elsight wants to change that with a new positioning technology designed to help uncrewed systems determine their location even when GPS is unavailable, jammed, or spoofed.
The Texas-based company has introduced a positioning capability that uses cellular network signals as an alternative source of location data.
The system is designed for autonomous platforms operating across air, land, and maritime environments, including places where satellite navigation cannot be trusted.
The timing is significant.
GPS jamming and spoofing have become growing concerns in military operations, with electronic warfare tools increasingly used to disrupt navigation and communications.
For drones and other autonomous vehicles, losing reliable positioning can complicate everything from route planning to mission execution.
There is also a practical advantage for existing customers.
The positioning capability is integrated into Elsight’s Halo platform, which combines cellular, satellite, and radio-frequency links to maintain connectivity for uncrewed systems.
Existing Halo customers can access the new feature through software or a feature unlock, without installing additional hardware.
There is one important distinction, however: this isn’t a universal replacement for GPS or a guarantee of uninterrupted positioning everywhere.

By using cellular infrastructure as an independent reference and checking GPS against it, Elsight is betting that resilience can be added without making autonomous platforms significantly more complicated.

evidenceRecords.text: Andrej Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI and now at Anthropic, sees a widening knowledge gap in AI.
The article Anthropic's Andrej Karpathy says "the external world has seen the preview" of what AI can actually do appeared first on The Decoder .
OpenAI co-founder and now Anthropic researcher Andrej Karpathy describes a widening gap in how people understand AI capabilities.
Only about 20 million professionals in math and programming use frontier models for work, by Karpathy's estimate.
Roughly 5,000 people worldwide have access to internal frontier systems.
Andrej Karpathy, co-founder of OpenAI, describes a rapidly widening gap in how people understand AI capabilities.
While the public treats chatbots like a better Google search, internal frontier systems are already tackling tasks that would take top experts years to complete.
Karpathy breaks down the user base of large language models into four levels.
About six billion people, roughly 75 percent of the global population, have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
Another one to two billion are casual users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products who treat them "a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc."
Even many professionals outside of math and code fall into this tier.

Executives and people in similar roles spend most of their time talking to other people, so "while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract," Karpathy writes.
The third tier covers an estimated 20 million people, about 0.2 percent of the world's population.

These are professional users of frontier-grade LLMs in math and code who see firsthand that "large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt." Karpathy lists "building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries" as examples.
"The external world has seen the preview," he writes.

evidenceRecords.text: Meta on Monday unveiled two new "frontier" artificial intelligence models called Wonder and Wonder Full, which the company claims perform at a level comparable to that of OpenAI's ChatGPT and Anthropic's Claude.
"Muse Spark was our first family of models, and now Muse Wonder is a much larger and more advanced class of models that brings us to the frontier," CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X.

Zuckerberg has pushed Meta to compete with leading AI labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, over the past year or so amid a race to win over customers and diversify beyond advertising, which has historically been its main source of revenue.
In June 2025, the company made a $14 billion investment in Scale AI, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and poached its co-founder Alexandr Wang as part of the deal.
Zuckerberg subsequently made Wang the company's chief AI officer overseeing its newly formed division called Superintelligence Labs.
Meta launched its Spark model in April, marking a departure from its open-source model known as Llama, which lagged behind the rest of the industry.
The new models can soon be used in Meta's new personal agent app, known as Muse, for paid subscribers only.
Wonder is "our largest and most capable model yet" and "rivals the big (boys)," Wang posted on X, presumably referring to leading labs OpenAI and Anthropic.

Last week, he sarcastically referred to Mukesh Ambani, one of India's richest people and chairman of Reliance Industries, as "Prime Minister Ambani" and accused his supporters of protecting a monopoly.
"Would you nonetheless consider allowing Starlink to compete?" Musk wrote on X, arguing that the service could bring internet access to underserved communities across India.
Rahul Gandhi, a leader of the opposition Indian National Congress, joined the discussion, writing: "Welcome to India, Elon.
Wait till you discover the other guy." Musk replied: "Thank you, Rahul.
This is indeed troubling."
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) accused Gandhi of championing Musk's interests, while party leaders defended the government's handling of the issue.
Speaking during the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi last week, Reliance Jio chairman Akash Ambani declined to comment on Musk's remarks.
He said: "I have no comments to make.
We want to keep our heads down and deliver value to our Indian consumers."
Akash, Mukesh Ambani's eldest son, also noted that Jio was progressing on its own end-to-end indigenous satellite broadband technology stack.
Meanwhile, Starlink — despite securing key approvals and signing distribution agreements with Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel — has yet to begin commercial operations in India.

The article Meta's new frontier model Muse Wonder Full breaks into the AI top tier appeared first on The Decoder .
Meta's two new models, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, close the gap to the leading frontier models.
Meta released its frontier model Muse Wonder in two variants, and both land among the best AI models available.
Muse Wonder Full scores 56 points on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3, while Muse Wonder hits 52.
Its predecessor, Muse Spark 1.3, sat at 48 points, which makes this a significant jump from what was a mid-tier model.
The biggest gains show up in agentic evaluations, tests that measure how well an AI model can handle complex tasks on its own.
On Terminal-Bench 4.0, performance jumped from 33 to 57 percent.
Muse Wonder Full places in the top three on six out of ten benchmarks overall, a strong result for Meta, which seems to have recovered after a weaker stretch with its open Llama models.
Both models support a one-million-token context window and accept text, images, video, and audio as input.
Muse Wonder is available through Meta's API and Muse Code, while Muse Wonder Full is currently limited to Muse Code users.
Muse Wonder will soon power the Muse app as well, starting with paying subscribers.
Over time, Meta plans to build specialized models from it for all users.
Both models show big improvements in coding.
Muse Wonder Full hits 68 points on the Coding Agents Index, tying Claude Code with Sonnet 5.5.
On the AA-Omniscience knowledge test, Muse Wonder Full manages only 30 points, and Muse Wonder gets 25.
Muse Wonder Full cuts its hallucination rate from 33 to 23 percent compared to its predecessor, the second-lowest among all models scoring at least 45 index points.
The company says Muse Wonder Full does better than expected on unfamiliar tasks that weren't part of training optimization, and credits this to a stronger base model.
On the Vals AI Index, Muse Wonder Full (Max) debuts at fifth place and beats all OpenAI models, according to Vals AI.
On ProofBench, a private benchmark for mathematical proofs, Muse Wonder Full solves 94 out of 100 problems, up from 58 for its predecessor.

evidenceRecords.text: Where Muse Spark aimed to be a lightweight model that could perform at low latency, the Wonder models are larger and said to be more capable, with higher benchmark scores and better results on complex tasks like coding.
Meta’s Superintelligence Lab released a pair of new state-of-the-art models on Monday, Muse Wonder and Muse Wonder Full, representing the company’s first attempt at a frontier model.
According to Meta’s testing (presented in the model card), Wonder and Wonder Full achieve comparable benchmark scores to Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra.
“Together, they mark the next step on our scaling ladder and a major leap toward personal superintelligence,” Meta’s blog post about the models reads.

That scale is reflected in the pricing: Accessed through the Meta Model API, Wonder will cost $4 per million input tokens and $20 per million output tokens, making it roughly equivalent in cost to GPT-6 Sol or Opus 5.5.
Notably, Wonder Full will only be available to Muse Code subscribers and will not be served through the API.
Both models will also be used to power the Muse agent.

In keeping with Meta’s interest in developing personal assistants that can perform tasks over a long period, the company placed particular emphasis on the new models’ ability to retain and synthesize information given by the user, a property Meta calls “active memory.”
To achieve better recall, Meta highlighted the MemoryBench benchmark, which challenges continual learning and memory construction frameworks.
According to the company’s testing, Muse Wonder now scores higher on MemoryBench than Fable, Opus, or Astra.
The new models are the first frontier model release since Scale AI founder Alexandr Wang restructured Meta’s AI efforts in August of last year.
Since then, Meta has released its lightweight Muse Spark model and Muse agent but has avoided the kind of state-of-the-art model releases OpenAI and Anthropic are known for.
